Assistant: That's really nice. Do you still keep in touch with him?

Passage: Despite the obvious star power, there's a distinct lack of voltage that runs throughout Keeping Up With The Joneses as the whole film just feels flat and insipid.
There's too much talent involved in Keeping Up With The Joneses for it not to be considered a disappointment.
Director Greg Mottola oversaw Superbad, Adventureland, and Paul, while The Hangover trilogy turned Zach Galifianakis into one of the biggest comedians in the world, even though his funniest material over the last 5 years has been on TV and the internet.
Plus, since Bridesmaids and his stellar supporting work on 30 Rock, Children's Hospital, Archer, and Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt, to name but a few, we've all been waiting for Jon Hamm to take the comedy world by storm with his own leading role. Isla Fisher is also an underrated comedy gem, and the inclusion of Wonder Woman herself Gal Gadot, making her debut in the comedy genre as a leading lady after a supporting role in Date Night, added some further wattage to the cast, too.
But despite the obvious star power, there's a distinct lack of voltage that runs throughout Keeping Up With The Joneses. The whole film just feels flat and insipid. Director Greg Mottola fails to add any flair or comedic idiosyncrasies to proceedings, and it all feels rather rudimentary and nothing more than a glorified TV production with a few impressive explosions.
Zach Galifianakis and Isla Fisher play Jeff and Karen Gaffney, a happily married suburban couple that are a little bored and now have two weeks of freedom as their kids have gone off to camp. Rather than repeatedly doing the no pants dance in an attempt to rekindle the spark in the marriage, Karen soon becomes obsessed with their new neighbors, Tim and Natalie Jones.
It's understandable really, since the pair are played by the downright gorgeous Jon Hamm and Gal Gadot. But as Jeff and Tim start to bond, Karen's paranoia grows and she follows Natalie and then convinces Jeff to break into the Joneses house where they discover that the latest additions to their neighborhood are actually spies. Karen and Jeff soon become embroiled in their investigation, which just so happens to be against Jeff's company and an individual that's selling secrets to the highest bidder.
Keeping Up With The Joneses actually gets from A to C, courtesy of B, rather well, with Karen and Jeff always aware that they're out of their depth and Galifianakis and Fisher adding enough terror and nerves to each scenario. At the same time, Gadot and Hamm are as cool, slick, and appealing as you'd imagine. You even buy why Karen and Jeff would be so integral to the final shoot-out, although it's hardly surprising that it unfolds in such a drab and dumb manner.
But while Keeping Up With The Joneses story structure is competent, it fails because in between its construction it's just nowhere near funny enough. It's especially a struggle at the start, as it takes too long for Keeping Up With The Joneses to build up any momentum and while it tries to do just that its jokes don't land and its comedic set-pieces unfold predictably.
There's Gadot excelling at darts when she's trying to remain inconspicuous, Fisher calling Gadot by accident because of voice-recognition, and Galifianakis banging an unconscious Fisher's head against a wall as he hurriedly tries to escape from the Joneses house after breaking in. It's all very yawn.
The leading foursome only spark into life when they're finally on the same page and the cool and composed Hamm and Gadot can spark off the erratic Galifianakis and Fisher. But that doesn't happen enough. When Gadot & Fisher and Hamm & Galifianakis are isolated in their own scenes as twosomes they each give their all and try to stretch and find laughs with their exchanges, but the material just isn't strong enough to provoke them.
At times you get a glimpse of what makes the leading quartet so appealing, but a caveat is always close behind. As per usual Zach Galifianakis is sweet, but he still feels restrained, especially considering how far he pushes the envelope with both Baskets and Between Two Ferns.
That's nowhere near enough to save Keeping Up With The Joneses, though, and once you've kept up with them you'll not only look to avoid them ever again but you'll tell your friends to do the same, too.

c35-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: • Remember the two licensed Call of Cthulhu computer games from Infogrames? The DOS point-and-click pixel-hunt adventures, 1993's Shadow of the Comet and its 1995 sequel, Prisoner of Ice? Me neither, but both were scripted by Alone in the Dark writer Hubert Chardot. Because all three games share minor characters, some fans consider them a loose trilogy.
• A recent low-budget French game, Frogwares' Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened, is a "first-person sleuther" that sends the great detective in search of kidnappers whose trail leads into a mystery with a thin, mock-Lovecraftian flavor. Though the game is tainted by StarForce copy protection, it - hey, wait, where are you going?
• The 2005 Xbox RPG Dark Corners of the Earth, another CoC license, is this list's real tragedy. The game got okay reviews (76% on Game Rankings), despite graphics badly dated by a crippling five-year gestation. "Dark Corners of the Earth is the best Cthulhu game I've played, and it was clearly a labor of love," says longtime CoC designer John Scott Tynes. "Walking the streets of Innsmouth was a blast. Unfortunately, it was ruined by excessive difficulty." The assault on the Marsh Hotel in Innsmouth was thrilling, he says, but "it lost its charm after the 20th time." Developer Headfirst Productions entered bankruptcy in March 2006, the same week the PC port appeared.
As in every game genre, there were other, aborted attempts: Tainted Legacy (cancelled); Headfirst's sequel to Dark Corners, Destiny's End (unpublished); and, most heartbreaking, a planned adaptation of Tynes's tabletop CoC supplement Delta Green. Now their nullity has spread, like a "Colour Out of Space," to the entire field. Fan site Calling Cthulhu, "Your Lovecraftian Gaming Source," shut down in April 2007. Wrote the admin, Nyarlathotep: "With Dark Corners of the Earth being released and no other real Lovecraftian games on the horizon, there is no point in keeping this site alive."
"The real problem with horror games is much the same as the problem with horror novels," Tynes says. "You can't maintain an intensity of terror across many hours. At best, you can alternate long stretches of plot with occasional moments of fright. The Silent Hill games have amazing art direction and concepts and feel really menacing - for about 15 minutes. Then it's just endless bludgeoning of demon dogs and monster nurses, and all the mood drains away. If Silent Hill was 20 minutes long, it'd be the scariest game ever made."
Though it enjoys fads, horror may be fated to remain a niche market. But it's interesting that the Lovecraftian games have succeeded almost inversely to their fidelity to the Mythos. The less Cthuloid they are, the more the market likes them. Why?
• You'd think a computer game has at least one leg up right away, given that - hurrah! - it can bypass the cliched HPL vocabulary (squamous rugose gibbous nefandous eldritch bloop bleep blup!). But a game nonetheless must depict monsters the author routinely calls "indescribable," not to mention weird other-worldly colors and "angles neither acute nor obtuse." So, text adventures aside, graphics are a challenge - at least until Microsoft releases its sanity-blasting trans-dimensional DirectX APIs.
• Speaking of sanity-shattering, exactly how does that work? Dark Corners took a shot: "A loss of sanity can be represented in many ways, such as hearing mysterious voices, hallucinating or suffering visual impairments (double vision and inability to focus)." It was probably worth a try. But a convincing simulation of insanity, even if possible, may not be desirable. Insanity implies a failure of perception, a distorted sense of available options. A player who acts based on false information, then suffers a horrible fate, won't feel insane - unless you consider him insane when he throws his controller at his television. User: • Remember the two licensed Call of Cthulhu computer games from Infogrames? The DOS point-and-click pixel-hunt adventures, 1993's Shadow of the Comet and its 1995 sequel, Prisoner of Ice? Me neither, but both were scripted by Alone in the Dark writer Hubert Chardot. Because all three games share minor characters, some fans consider them a loose trilogy.
• A recent low-budget French game, Frogwares' Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened, is a "first-person sleuther" that sends the great detective in search of kidnappers whose trail leads into a mystery with a thin, mock-Lovecraftian flavor. Though the game is tainted by StarForce copy protection, it - hey, wait, where are you going?
• The 2005 Xbox RPG Dark Corners of the Earth, another CoC license, is this list's real tragedy. The game got okay reviews (76% on Game Rankings), despite graphics badly dated by a crippling five-year gestation. "Dark Corners of the Earth is the best Cthulhu game I've played, and it was clearly a labor of love," says longtime CoC designer John Scott Tynes. "Walking the streets of Innsmouth was a blast. Unfortunately, it was ruined by excessive difficulty." The assault on the Marsh Hotel in Innsmouth was thrilling, he says, but "it lost its charm after the 20th time." Developer Headfirst Productions entered bankruptcy in March 2006, the same week the PC port appeared.
As in every game genre, there were other, aborted attempts: Tainted Legacy (cancelled); Headfirst's sequel to Dark Corners, Destiny's End (unpublished); and, most heartbreaking, a planned adaptation of Tynes's tabletop CoC supplement Delta Green. Now their nullity has spread, like a "Colour Out of Space," to the entire field. Fan site Calling Cthulhu, "Your Lovecraftian Gaming Source," shut down in April 2007. Wrote the admin, Nyarlathotep: "With Dark Corners of the Earth being released and no other real Lovecraftian games on the horizon, there is no point in keeping this site alive."
"The real problem with horror games is much the same as the problem with horror novels," Tynes says. "You can't maintain an intensity of terror across many hours. At best, you can alternate long stretches of plot with occasional moments of fright. The Silent Hill games have amazing art direction and concepts and feel really menacing - for about 15 minutes. Then it's just endless bludgeoning of demon dogs and monster nurses, and all the mood drains away. If Silent Hill was 20 minutes long, it'd be the scariest game ever made."
Though it enjoys fads, horror may be fated to remain a niche market. But it's interesting that the Lovecraftian games have succeeded almost inversely to their fidelity to the Mythos. The less Cthuloid they are, the more the market likes them. Why?
• You'd think a computer game has at least one leg up right away, given that - hurrah! - it can bypass the cliched HPL vocabulary (squamous rugose gibbous nefandous eldritch bloop bleep blup!). But a game nonetheless must depict monsters the author routinely calls "indescribable," not to mention weird other-worldly colors and "angles neither acute nor obtuse." So, text adventures aside, graphics are a challenge - at least until Microsoft releases its sanity-blasting trans-dimensional DirectX APIs.
• Speaking of sanity-shattering, exactly how does that work? Dark Corners took a shot: "A loss of sanity can be represented in many ways, such as hearing mysterious voices, hallucinating or suffering visual impairments (double vision and inability to focus)." It was probably worth a try. But a convincing simulation of insanity, even if possible, may not be desirable. Insanity implies a failure of perception, a distorted sense of available options. A player who acts based on false information, then suffers a horrible fate, won't feel insane - unless you consider him insane when he throws his controller at his television. Assistant: There have been several failed attempts at Lovecraftian game adaptations, including Tainted Legacy (cancelled), Destiny's End (unpublished), and a planned adaptation of John Scott Tynes's tabletop CoC supplement Delta Green. The nullity of these projects has spread throughout the industry, with fan sites shutting down due to a lack of new Lovecraftian games in development. The real problem with horror games, according to Tynes, is the difficulty of maintaining an intensity of terror across many hours. Additionally, the less fidelity Lovecraftian games have to the Mythos, the more successful they are in the market. Graphics are a challenge in depicting Lovecraft's indescribable monsters, and a convincing simulation of insanity may not be desirable for gameplay purposes.

Assistant: Sure, here are a few Lovecraftian games that are currently available to play:

1. "The Sinking City" by Frogwares: This game immerses players in the world of Lovecraft's stories, with a heavy emphasis on investigation, exploration, and non-linear encounters.

3. "Sunless Sea" by Failbetter Games: This game is set in a Lovecraftian version of the Victorian Era, with players piloting a ship through a surreal and dangerous underworld filled with monsters and other hidden dangers.

4. "Darkest Dungeon" by Red Hook Studios: This game is a roguelike RPG set in a Lovecraftian world, where players must lead a team of explorers through a series of increasingly challenging dungeons filled with horrors and impossible odds.

5. "Conarium" by Zoetrope Interactive: This game is a psychological horror experience that explores the themes of Lovecraft's stories, with players exploring an Antarctic research base that hides secrets and horrors beyond imagination.

These games offer different styles of gameplay and immersion into the world of Lovecraft's stories, so choose the one that suits your preferences the most.

Assistant: Introducing Our Latest Product Feature – Automated Alerts!

We’re excited to announce the release of our newest feature for our platform – Automated Alerts! 

With Automated Alerts, you can now set up customized notifications and alerts that are triggered based on specific criteria. This will allow you to stay on top of important events and data within your organization without having to constantly monitor your platform. 

Here’s how it works:

First, you simply define the conditions that will trigger the alert. For example, you could set up an alert that would notify you when a new lead is added to your CRM, or when a customer’s account balance goes above a certain threshold.

Next, you choose how you want to receive the alert – via email, SMS, or in-app notification.

Once you save the alert, the platform automatically monitors your data and triggers the alert whenever the specified conditions are met. 

This feature is especially useful for teams that want to stay on top of critical events, such as sales teams who want to be notified immediately when a new lead is added, or finance teams who want to be alerted when a customer’s account balance becomes delinquent. 

In addition, Automated Alerts can help improve efficiency and reduce the likelihood of errors in your business processes. For example, if you set up an alert to notify your shipping team when an order is placed with a specific shipping address, you can ensure that the order gets shipped to the correct location every time.

We hope you find Automated Alerts to be a valuable addition to our platform. As always, please reach out to our support team if you have any questions about setting up and using this new feature.

User: Here is a piece of text: A reader of my “Perennial Publius” series has written to ask what edition of the Federalist I would recommend. Quite a while ago another asked why I wasn’t linking to each essay in some online location (there are multiple websites containing the whole Federalist series), and my answer to him was that I wanted people to go out and buy a copy of the Federalist in a book if they were really interested. So, what book?
There are lots of editions; I have several but not all. Of current editions worth using, there’s Charles Kesler’s Mentor paperback, a new version of the old pocket-sized standby edited by Clinton Rossiter, but with Charles’s wonderful new introduction. The Modern Library edition is recently updated with a new introduction by Robert Scigliano, also quite good. The Liberty Fund edition edited by George W. Carey and the late James McClellan is a unique reprint of the 1818 Gideon edition (Madison’s favorite), while scholars frequently rely on the Jacob E. Cooke critical edition from Wesleyan University Press, still in print since 1961, but the most expensive on the market.
In my classroom this semester, and at my elbow for the Publius series here, though, is the new edition by the English historian J.R. Pole, from Hackett Publishing. It’s affordable, based on the authoritative Cooke edition, with Pole’s highly useful annotations, and printed in a size and format that please the eye more than most (if less sturdily bound for hard use than Liberty Fund’s equally affordable volume).
There are others. These, in my view, are the good ones.

Assistant: Sure, the website for Hackett Publishing is https://www.hackettpublishing.com.

Assistant: I'd be happy to help. What type of shows are you into? Are you a fan of fiction, non-fiction, or a mix of both?
User: I'd say I'm more into non-fiction. I love learning new things and expanding my knowledge.
Assistant: Non-fiction is a great way to go. There are so many fascinating documentaries out there. Have you watched any documentaries recently that caught your attention?
User: Actually, I've been meaning to get back into watching documentaries, but I haven't had the chance to lately. What are some popular documentary topics that people are into these days?
Assistant: Well, it seems like documentaries about history, science, and technology are always in high demand. But I've also noticed a surge in documentaries about ancient civilizations and lost cities. People seem to be really interested in uncovering the secrets of the past.
User: That sounds really interesting. I've always been fascinated by ancient civilizations. I think it's because I had a great history teacher in school who made the subject come alive.
Assistant: Having a great teacher can definitely make a big difference. Ancient civilizations are fascinating because they were often so advanced for their time, and yet, they also had their own unique struggles and challenges. What is it about ancient civilizations that you find particularly captivating?
User: I think it's the fact that they were able to build such complex societies and achieve great things, but ultimately, many of them fell apart. I often find myself wondering what led to their downfall.
Assistant: That's a great question. There are so many factors that can contribute to the rise and fall of ancient empires. Sometimes it's due to external factors like wars or environmental disasters, while other times it's due to internal factors like corruption or mismanagement.
User: I often find myself watching documentaries about the rise and fall of ancient empires. I'm particularly fascinated by the Roman Empire and the Egyptians. What do you think is the most interesting aspect of these empires?
Assistant: I think one of the most interesting aspects is the way they were able to create such lasting legacies. I mean, think about it - the Romans built roads, aqueducts, and buildings that are still standing today, while the Egyptians built pyramids that are still considered some of the greatest architectural achievements of all time. It's amazing to think about how they were able to accomplish so much with the limited technology and resources they had.
User: That's so true. And I think it's also interesting to note that both of these empires were able to adapt and evolve over time, which helped them to survive for so long. But ultimately, they both fell victim to internal decay and external pressures.
Assistant: Exactly. It's a great reminder that even the greatest civilizations can fall if they're not careful. But at the same time, it's also a testament to the ingenuity and resilience of the human spirit. We can learn a lot from the successes and failures of ancient empires, and apply those lessons to our own lives and societies today.
User: Absolutely. I think that's one of the reasons why I find documentaries about ancient empires so fascinating. They're not just entertaining - they're also educational and thought-provoking.
Assistant: Well, if you're looking for more documentaries to watch, I'd be happy to recommend some. There are plenty of great shows out there that explore the rise and fall of ancient empires in depth. Would you like some recommendations?
User: Hey, what's your take on modern movies and books? Do you think they're getting more creative or just reusing old ideas?

User: Timeless, that's a great point. I've noticed that some of the most popular movies and books have roots in ancient myths. What do you think makes those myths so appealing to modern audiences?
Assistant: Well, I believe it's because ancient myths tap into fundamental human emotions and experiences. They deal with universal themes like love, power, and the struggle between good and evil. Those themes are just as relevant today as they were back then.
User: That makes sense. I've always been fascinated by how myths can be retold and reinterpreted in different ways. Do you think that's part of their enduring appeal?
Assistant: Absolutely. Myths are often open to multiple interpretations, which makes them versatile and adaptable. It's like they have a built-in flexibility that allows them to be reimagined and reinterpreted for different cultures and time periods.
User: I've been trying to learn more about the connections between ancient mythology and modern storytelling. Do you have any recommendations for where to start?
Assistant: Actually, there are many great resources out there. You could try reading some of the classic myths themselves, like Homer's epics or Ovid's Metamorphoses. Or, if you prefer something more modern, you could look into books that explore the connections between mythology and popular culture.
User: That sounds like a great idea. I've actually been thinking of taking a course to deepen my understanding of ancient mythology and its impact on modern storytelling.

You'll likely get to explore different mythological traditions, analyze case studies of modern stories that draw on mythology, and maybe even try your hand at creating your own myth-inspired stories.
User: Exactly! I'm actually taking an online course on ancient mythology right now. We're exploring how myths have influenced everything from literature to film to video games. It's been really eye-opening to see just how pervasive mythological themes are in modern media.
Assistant: That sounds like an amazing course! I'm sure you're learning a lot about the different ways myths can be used and reinterpreted. Are there any particular mythological themes or stories that you're finding especially interesting or relevant to modern storytelling?
User: One thing that's really struck me is how often the hero's journey appears in modern stories. I mean, it's everywhere – from Star Wars to Harry Potter to The Lord of the Rings. It's amazing how that one mythological pattern can be used in so many different ways.
Assistant: The hero's journey is definitely a powerful and versatile mythological theme. It taps into our deep-seated desires for adventure, transformation, and triumph over adversity. And it's interesting that you mention how it can be used in different ways – that's one of the key things about mythology, is that it can be adapted and reinterpreted to fit different contexts and cultures.
User: Yeah, and I think that's part of why mythology remains so relevant today. It's not just a bunch of old stories – it's a way of understanding ourselves and the world around us. By tapping into mythological themes and patterns, modern storytellers can create stories that resonate with audiences on a deep level.
Assistant: Well said! Mythology may be ancient, but it's still a powerful tool for storytelling and self-discovery. And it sounds like your course is giving you a great appreciation for the many ways mythology continues to shape and influence modern storytelling.

Assistant: Pergamon was known for its powerful military and innovative defensive strategies that set it apart from other ancient cities of the time. The city was strategically located on a steep hilltop, which provided a natural defense against invading forces. In addition, Pergamon was surrounded by deep valleys, making it difficult to approach the city from any direction.

Pergamon's military was also renowned for its use of innovative weapons and tactics. The city-state was one of the first to adopt the use of siege engines, including the ballista and the catapult, which gave its soldiers a significant advantage on the battlefield. Pergamon also had a highly trained cavalry unit, which was used to outflank and attack enemy forces.

Moreover, Pergamon maintained a powerful navy that dominated the Aegean Sea and protected the city from sea-born attacks. The city also had a sophisticated system of fortifications and walls that provided further protection.

User: Provide a comprehensive explanation on the ways in which a vending machine keeps track of its inventory, including the technologies or systems used, the data collected, and how it is analyzed to determine when to restock or replenish the items. Your response should also highlight any potential challenges or limitations of inventory tracking in vending machines and potential solutions to address them.
Assistant: Vending machines are equipped with a variety of technologies and systems that allow them to keep track of their inventory levels. These systems typically involve sensors, microprocessors, and software that are designed to monitor the quantity of items available for purchase and communicate this information to the vending machine owner/operator.

One common technology used in vending machine inventory tracking is the use of weight sensors. These sensors can be placed on each shelf or compartment within the vending machine and are used to detect changes in weight as items are purchased or restocked. This information is then transmitted to the vending machine's microprocessor and analyzed to determine if a particular item needs to be restocked.

Another popular technology used in vending machine inventory tracking is the use of RFID (Radio Frequency Identification) chips. Each item within the machine is equipped with a small, embedded RFID chip that can be read by sensors within the vending machine. As items are purchased or restocked, this information is transmitted to the microprocessor and analyzed to determine when a particular item needs to be restocked.

Other data collected by the vending machine may include sales data, machine usage data, and even environmental data such as temperature, humidity, and light levels. This information can be used to analyze customer behavior and preferences, as well as to optimize the vending machine's inventory management and restocking processes.

One potential challenge with inventory tracking in vending machines is the issue of accuracy. Weight sensors can be affected by external factors such as vibrations or changes in temperature, while RFID chips can become damaged or malfunction over time. Machine malfunctions or power outages can also cause inaccuracies in data collection. To address these challenges, some vending machine operators may use multiple tracking technologies or conduct regular maintenance and calibration of sensors and software.

In conclusion, vending machines use various technologies and systems to keep track of inventory levels. The data collected by these systems is analyzed to determine when items need to be restocked or replenished. Challenges such as accuracy can be mitigated with regular maintenance and use of multiple tracking technologies.
User: Can you please provide more details on how sales data and machine usage data are utilized in inventory management? Also, are there any new technologies being developed to improve vending machine inventory tracking?

Sales data can help operators understand which items are most popular among customers and adjust their inventory accordingly. They can also use this data to test new products or promotions, as well as adjust prices based on demand. Machine usage data can provide insights into how often the machine is being used and when it may need to be restocked. For example, if a vending machine consistently runs out of a certain item at certain times of day, an operator can adjust inventory levels to make sure the item is always available during peak hours. In terms of new technologies, there are a few that are emerging in the vending machine industry that could improve inventory tracking. One of these is computer vision technology, which uses cameras and machine learning algorithms to track inventory levels in real time. This can eliminate the need for weight sensors or RFID chips and provide more accurate data about inventory levels. Another technology that is currently being developed is blockchain. This could potentially be used to create more secure and transparent supply chains for vending machine inventory management. For example, it could be used to track the origin and movement of products, as well as monitor inventory levels and automate ordering and restocking processes. Overall, the use of sales data, machine usage data, and emerging technologies are all important factors in optimizing inventory management in vending machines. By continually monitoring and adjusting inventory levels, operators can ensure that customers always have access to their favorite products and maximize profits.
